title: Levin v. Halston Limited
lead: A mother alleges that her custom wedding-occasion dress arrived badly made, but her understandable disappointment does not sustain the particular contract damages she seeks.

actors.name: Mrs. Myron Levin
actors.role: Purchaser seeking a dress for herself to wear at her daughter’s wedding.

actors.name: Halston Limited
actors.role: Designer’s business, seller and movant challenging the mental-suffering claim.

proceedings: Levin sued for the deposit and mental anguish.
On Halston’s motion, the New York City Civil Court dismissed only the mental-suffering cause.
limits: The purchaser, not her daughter, was the intended wearer. Alleged defects were considered favorably on a motion and were not adjudicated facts. The reported decision does not dispose of the separate deposit request or certify current New York law.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Levin orders a dress for her daughter’s wedding
sections.cue: What did she arrange and what additional visits did she allege?
paragraphs: Mrs. Myron Levin of Highland Park, Illinois, wanted a custom-made Halston dress for herself to wear at her daughter’s wedding. In February 1975 she visited Halston Limited’s New York showroom, selected a possible dress, had her measurements taken, and received fabric samples. At the end of April she ordered it and sent a $335 deposit.

She alleged that Halston lost the measurements and required her to fly back to New York. She made a third trip in June for a fitting. The dress arrived before June 20, as promised, but she was deeply dissatisfied with what she received.

sections.title: The delivered dress leads to a replacement and two requested remedies
sections.cue: Which failures remained allegations at this stage?
paragraphs: Levin described an uneven hem, a badly fitting neckline and capelet, and poor packing. Her letter expressed dismay that the workmanship bore the designer’s label. With fewer than six weeks before the wedding, she could not return to New York to have it remade. The dress apparently went back and forth between Illinois and New York, and payment of the remaining $345 was stopped.

She hurriedly obtained another dress and never wore the disputed one. She then sued for return of her deposit and for mental anguish. Halston moved to dismiss the mental-anguish cause as legally insufficient. The court considered her account favorably for that motion; it did not try and resolve each alleged defect.

sections.title: Sherman explains why sympathy does not supply this category of damages
sections.cue: What exceptions did the court consider?
paragraphs: Judge Burton S. Sherman recognized the importance of Levin’s daughter’s wedding and the disappointment reflected in her letter. He nevertheless applied the general rule against recovering mental-suffering damages for breach of contract.

The authorities he cited recognized a few exceptions involving fiduciary or quasi-fiduciary contractual relationships, such as hotel and guest, carrier and passenger, or amusement park and patron, coupled with tortious conduct. He found no such exception applicable to this purchase. Ordering a personalized dress did not itself establish that kind of relationship or tort liability.

Sherman also invoked the contract-damages principle associated with Hadley: recovery is limited to natural and probable consequences reasonably foreseeable at formation. He concluded that the claimed mental suffering did not qualify here. His brief analysis did not make a finding that Halston had been unaware of the wedding.

sections.title: The first cause is dismissed without a reported resolution of the deposit
paragraphs: On October 3, 1977, the Civil Court of the City of New York, Special Term, New York County, dismissed the first cause of action for mental suffering and directed judgment accordingly. No separate opinion appears.

The reported ruling did not decide that the dress had been properly made, order return of the deposit, determine the cost of the replacement dress, or enter a completed damages award. The separately pleaded deposit claim was outside the disposition described in this opinion.
